sm: The episode opens with a short video about how the covers for a fantasy book series called Ashtown were made. An illustrator and a block print artist describe going through hundreds of styles before settling on a handcrafted woodblock look, with layers of ink, paper textures, maps and illustrations inside. They say the goal was a human touch that digital work can't fully imitate, in keeping with the aim of reigniting the American imagination. Then the hosts, including Jared Longshore and Wade, welcome listeners to the mid-November edition of Doug Wilson and Friends and chat briefly about an upcoming episode of Wade's show.

The hosts say today's topic is why stories matter for building culture, and why maps, graphs and statistics aren't enough. They point out that most of the Bible is narrative and poetry, and that Jesus taught mostly through parables rather than systematic categories. A story sticks in memory, as with an anecdote about a panicking Stoic from Augustine's City of God, and it motivates, as when you tell a child to be like Sam Gamgee. They worry that a scrolling, meme-driven culture reduces characters to thirty-second clips and reaction GIFs, so people lose the long journey with a character that makes the story shape them.

The conversation turns to why evangelicals and conservatives lean on graphs and polls. One speaker says people assume everyone is persuaded by statistics, but fiction is inescapable, and evangelicals already consume fiction, such as Amish romance and Left Behind, that doesn't edify fully. Reading fiction takes a counter-cultural attitude toward a busy modern life, and one suggestion is to start with the Old Testament stories and let them shape how you see real situations. Good stories contain a turn where things look doomed and then are not. They say Left Behind has the lonely last stand but lacks any vision of victory, and that Christians may fear winning.

The hosts discuss what kinds of stories conservatives need, noting that rebellion has spread everywhere, so wholesome material is harder to find than in Chesterton's day of penny dreadfuls. One host says stories teach setup and payoff, and that life is not constant dopamine hits. Another says God loves cliffhangers, taking Abraham and Israel right to the edge, and that we learn to enjoy suspense in novels before we can in life. They contrast this with the forbidden divination in Israel, comparing it to the modern appetite for forecasts and polls. We are meant to live in the sentence, with God's laws and stories rather than a preview of the future.

They say stories also build shared culture, since references like Narnia let families and nations communicate, and that immersion in stories protects against what one host calls squid ink: people casting every event as an op by some bond villain. They read a post by CJ Engel saying conservatives raise sons on Lord of the Rings, Narnia and Richard the Lionheart, then scold them for acting. Speakers answer that Lord of the Rings is a warning about the treachery of power, with every member of the fellowship tested by the ring. Some young men are rightly scolded, like Boromir, and the situation is not simple. One host doubts these kids actually know the stories deeply.

Continuing that thought, the hosts argue that we know hero names and memes but are not steeped in the actual heroism of the books. To read the times well, they say, you should keep asking the disciples' question, Lord, is it I. Mr. Collins in Pride and Prejudice is funny because he is the one person who doesn't know he is Mr. Collins, and readers who always cast themselves as David never ask whether they are Saul. Good fiction asks you to sit in the passenger seat and be taught. They then ask what Americans should do so as not to end up like Europe, which they describe as further along in secularism and immigration.

One host answers that stories include history and biography, and these show that bad action breeds reaction, which breeds overreaction, so he advises acting rather than reacting, as his father taught him. A reactionary is impatient, while a reformer thinks in centuries. Another host tells of a Romanian teacher in the Ceausescu era who was given The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe at the British consulate and recognized her own country in Narnia's endless winter. It was translated and circulated secretly, which is why Romanian universities have C. S. Lewis study centers. Tolkien's ideas came from the leaf mold of a mind formed by centuries of learning.

They say the First World War wiped out many in the generation shaped by classical Christian education, so we need to replant the forest by reading great stories to children and putting them in schools that honor them. One host says conservatives often forget America is still the most powerful nation, and should stop being shrill, comparing the worried right to Saul and recommending David's patience in sparing Saul in the cave. They cite the Pentagon honoring a soldier after an incident at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier as a story with the right arc. The first priority, they say, is remembering the creator-creature distinction, so right and wrong are not set by consensus.

The final part says that we build tombs for the prophets who stood against tyrants, and that you may have to take a stand before anyone will join you, citing Dabney on conservatism that follows radicalism to perdition. For recommended reading, they mention Nate's Ashtown series, Lord of the Rings, Narnia and A Wrinkle in Time, and above all Genesis, Exodus, Samuel, Judges, Ezra and Nehemiah. They note that Abraham's story is a map of Israel's later story, and they praise the account of Athaliah, in which Jehoiada and Jehosheba patiently hide the child Joash and then strike cleanly. Obadiah hiding prophets shows the same pattern: wait faithfully, and when the moment comes you will know.
